lines.text: Drowsy driving is impaired driving.
Plan long drives.
Know the warning signs.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson on dangerous behaviors. We start with drowsy driving. The manual says drowsy driving counts as impaired driving, and it gives a plan for long drives, a list of tricks that do not work, a list of warning signs, and steps to prevent drowsiness before a trip. It also tells you what to do if you spot a drowsy driver on the road. By the end of this lesson you should be able to describe the plan for a long drive, explain why the common tricks fail, name the warning signs, and say what to do about another driver who looks drowsy, including what information to give the police.

lines.text: Rest stop at least every two hours.
Nap ten to twenty minutes at a safe spot.
Share driving; avoid ten p.m. to six a.m.

narration.text: Cap long drives with a rest stop at least every two hours. Nap ten to twenty minutes at a safe spot. Share wheel time with a companion, so that a rested person is driving. And avoid driving in the window from ten p.m. to six a.m. These four steps are the manual's plan against drowsiness on a long trip: regular stops, short naps, a rested driver, and avoiding the late-night hours. Before the trip, the manual also says to bank sleep first, skip alcohol and heavy meals, and mind medicines that can dull you. Put together, prevention starts before you leave and continues with breaks along the way.

lines.text: Cracked windows, gum, loud radio.
Caffeine or energy drinks.
None of them fend off drowsiness.

narration.text: Here is the trap: trying to fight sleepiness with a cracked window, chewing gum, loud radio, or caffeine and energy drinks. The manual says none of these can fend off drowsiness, and drowsy driving counts as impaired driving. Real drowsy defense means two-hour breaks with short naps and rested drivers, while windows, gum, radio and caffeine only pretend to help. So if you notice yourself reaching for one of those tricks, treat it as a sign that you need a real defense instead: a safe place to stop and nap, or a rested companion to take over. The manual is clear that these tricks do not fend off drowsiness.

lines.text: Yawns, nods, heavy eyelids.
Lost miles, skipped signs, stray lanes.
Shoulder runs and rumble strip hits.

narration.text: The manual lists the warning signs of drowsiness: yawns, nods, heavy eyelids, lost miles you cannot remember, skipped signs, straying from your lane, running onto the shoulder, and hitting rumble strips. Drowsiness clouds judgment and can drop you asleep. Put as a contrast: yawns, nods and rumble strips warn of drowsiness that has already arrived, while banking sleep and avoiding alcohol and heavy meals stop it before the trip. So the signs are a late warning. By the time you hit a rumble strip, drowsiness is already affecting your driving, and the right response is the real defense from the last slide.

lines.text: Eyelids heavy.
Opens a window.
Enough?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Cal feels his eyelids getting heavy on a long drive, so he opens a window and turns up the radio. Will that fend off his drowsiness? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Cracked windows, gum, loud radio, and caffeine or energy drinks cannot fend off drowsiness. Heavy eyelids are a warning sign that drowsiness has already arrived. Cal should stop at a safe spot and nap ten to twenty minutes, or let a rested companion drive. On long trips he should also plan a rest stop at least every two hours. Every two hours, stop; caffeine is not sleep.

lines.text: Make a safe stop, or have a passenger call police.
Give location, vehicle and actions.

narration.text: To close the lesson, what to do about someone else. If you spot a drowsy driver, make a safe stop, or have a passenger call the police, giving the location, the vehicle and what the driver is doing. To recap: drowsy driving counts as impaired driving. On long drives, stop at least every two hours, nap ten to twenty minutes at a safe spot, share the wheel with a rested companion, and avoid the ten p.m. to six a.m. window. Windows, gum, radio and caffeine cannot fend off drowsiness. Watch for yawns, nods, heavy eyelids, lost miles, stray lanes and rumble strip hits, and prevent drowsiness by banking sleep and skipping alcohol and heavy meals.

why_how.text: BAC limits differ by age, and even one drink raises crash odds.
Only time sobers you, and drugs, legal ones included, can impair driving and multiply alcohol's effect.

reasoning.text: Under twenty-one, point zero two up to point zero eight means illegal consumption, and point zero eight or more means DUI.

result.text: Tara's point zero four counts as illegal consumption.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a driver under twenty-one is legal below point zero eight.

correction.text: Adults meet DUI at point zero eight, while drivers under twenty-one meet illegal consumption from point zero two and DUI at point zero eight.

memory_support.text: Twenty-one and up: point zero eight; under: point zero two.

prompt.text: Tara, nineteen, has a BAC of point zero four. What does that count as?

lines.text: BAC limits by age.
One drink, seven times the odds.
Drugs and sober rides.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on alcohol and drugs. The manual sets BAC limits that differ by age, and it explains that impairment alone can lead to a DUI conviction even below the limit. It gives figures on how common drunk driving is late at night and how much one drink raises crash odds. It explains what counts as one drink and what does and does not sober you up. It tells you to book a sober ride before a drinking event, warns that alcohol and drugs multiply each other, and lists the many drugs, legal ones included, that can dull your driving. By the end you should know the limits and the myths the manual rejects.

lines.text: Twenty-one and up: DUI at point zero eight or higher.
Impairment alone can convict lower.
Drug impairment draws DUI-grade penalties.

narration.text: Drivers twenty-one and up reach DUI at a BAC of point zero eight or higher, and impairment alone can bring a conviction at a lower level. Under twenty-one, a BAC from point zero two up to point zero eight means illegal consumption, and point zero eight or more means DUI. Drug impairment draws DUI-grade penalties. Put as a contrast: adults meet DUI at point zero eight, while drivers under twenty-one meet illegal consumption from point zero two and DUI at point zero eight. So the point zero eight line is the DUI line for everyone, and drivers under twenty-one face a second, lower line at point zero two for illegal consumption.

lines.text: Ten PM to two AM: three of ten drivers drunk.
Nearly half of DUI arrests: social to moderate drinkers.
One drink: crash odds seven times sober.

narration.text: From ten PM to two AM, three of ten drivers are drunk, and over a third of them are coming from someone's home. Nearly fifty percent of DUI arrests involve social to moderate drinkers. Over a lifetime, the chance of being in an alcohol-related crash is a coin flip. And one drink dents vision, judgment and coordination, and multiplies crash odds seven times compared with being sober. So the manual's figures say that drunk driving is common late at night, that it is not limited to heavy drinkers, and that even one drink changes your driving. And since drinking erodes the very judgment you need, the manual says to make the no-drive decision before the first sip.

lines.text: Twelve ounces of beer equals a shot or a five-ounce glass of wine.
Coffee, cold showers and workouts do not sober you.
Decide not to drive before the first sip.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People believe coffee, a cold shower or a workout can sober them up. The manual says only passing time sobers you. It also says that twelve ounces of beer equal a shot of liquor or a five-ounce glass of wine, so equal pours of each affect you the same. And because drinking erodes the very judgment you need to decide, make the no-drive decision before the first sip. Put as a contrast: only time sobers a drinker, past coffee and cold showers, matching how only real rest beats drowsiness, past caffeine. In both cases, the quick fixes do not work, and only time or rest does.

lines.text: Book a sober ride before drinking.
Alcohol plus drugs multiplies both.
Nearly every drug can dull driving.

narration.text: Before a drinking event, book a sober ride, either alternate transport or a sober driver. Alcohol stacked on drugs multiplies both, so a single drink on top of even aspirin or cold medicine can hit like several. Nearly every drug can dull driving, legal ones included: headache, hay fever, cold, allergy and nerve pills, syrups, drops, sprays and tablets can slow you. Marijuana stays DUI-illegal behind the wheel, even past twenty-one. Read labels, ask your pharmacist or doctor, and treat no drug as harmless. So street drugs impair, and so do headache, cold and allergy remedies, plus marijuana behind the wheel.

lines.text: Driver age nineteen.
BAC of point zero four.
What does it count as?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Tara is nineteen and is stopped with a BAC of point zero four. What does that count as? Work it out before reading on. The answer is illegal consumption. Under twenty-one, a BAC from point zero two up to point zero eight means illegal consumption, and point zero eight or more means DUI. If Tara were twenty-one or older, point zero eight would be the DUI line, though impairment alone can convict at a lower level. If you answered that she was legal because she was under point zero eight, you applied the adult rule to a driver under twenty-one. Twenty-one and up: point zero eight; under: point zero two.

lines.text: Point zero eight; under twenty-one, point zero two.
One drink: seven times the odds.
Only time sobers; book a sober ride.

narration.text: To close the lesson: drivers twenty-one and up reach DUI at point zero eight or higher, and impairment alone can convict lower. Under twenty-one, point zero two up to point zero eight is illegal consumption, and point zero eight or more is DUI. One drink dents vision, judgment and coordination and multiplies crash odds seven times. Twelve ounces of beer equal a liquor shot or a five-ounce glass of wine, and only time sobers you. Book a sober ride before a drinking event, remember that alcohol and drugs multiply each other, and treat no drug as harmless, legal ones included. Marijuana stays DUI-illegal behind the wheel past twenty-one.

why_how.text: Driving needs your whole attention, and Virginia bars holding a phone at the wheel.
Distraction causes roughly seventeen percent of Virginia crashes, and simple habits prevent it.

scenario.text: Lia wants to type a new address into her phone's map app while driving.

reasoning.text: Navigation use stands only while entering nothing and holding nothing.

result.text: Lia pulls fully over to enter the address before driving on.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is legal to type into a navigation app while driving.

correction.text: Holding any wireless device breaks the law outside emergencies and parked stops, while hands-free navigation without typing stays legal.

prompt.text: Lia wants to type an address into her phone's map while driving. Is that legal?

answer.text: No. Navigation use stands only while entering nothing and holding nothing.

rationale.text: Hands-free navigation without typing is legal, but holding or typing into a device is not.

title.text: Eyes and mind on the road

lines.text: Your whole attention.
The handheld device law.
How distraction causes crashes.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on distracted driving. The manual says driving wants your whole attention. It sets a clear rule for phones, computers and similar devices, and Virginia law bars holding a phone or wireless device at the wheel, with a few narrow exceptions. The manual also explains how distraction leads to crashes, and it gives a share of Virginia crashes that distraction causes. Finally it lists habits that prevent distraction before you start driving. By the end of this lesson you should know when a device may be used, what the navigation rule allows, and the three habits that keep your attention on driving.

lines.text: Shelve phones, computers and similar devices.
Except to report a crash or emergency.
Pull fully over before any distracting act.

narration.text: Driving wants your whole attention. Shelve phones, computers and similar devices, except to report a crash or emergency. And pull fully over before any distracting act. So the manual's default is that devices are put away while you drive, and the only exception it names for using one is reporting a crash or an emergency. Anything else that would take your attention waits until you have pulled fully over. The next slide turns that advice into law: Virginia bars holding a phone or wireless device at the wheel, with only a few exceptions.

lines.text: No holding a phone at the wheel.
Exceptions: driver emergency, lawfully parked or stopped.
Navigation only while entering nothing and holding nothing.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver uses a phone for navigation and assumes that makes it legal to hold the phone or type into it while driving. It does not. Virginia bars holding a phone or wireless device at the wheel, except in a driver emergency or while lawfully parked or stopped. Navigation use is allowed only while you are entering nothing and holding nothing. Holding any wireless device breaks the law outside emergencies and parked stops, while hands-free navigation without typing stays legal. So if you need to type an address, pull fully over first. The memory line for this rule is: hold nothing, enter nothing.

lines.text: Roughly seventeen percent of Virginia crashes.
The car strays; recognition lags; an emergency move follows.
Young drivers add weak control and tailgating.

narration.text: Distraction causes roughly seventeen percent of Virginia crashes. The pattern the manual describes is this: the straying car enters danger, recognition lags by precious seconds, and an emergency move follows. Young distracted drivers add weak control, tailgating and failures to yield on top of their lack of experience. So the cost of distraction is time: the seconds you lose before you recognize a hazard. The prevention habits on the next slide are designed to keep those seconds. Distraction eats recognition seconds behind seventeen percent of crashes, while eyes-up, preset and phone-down habits buy them back.

lines.text: Eyes on the road, hands on the wheel.
Preset every control before rolling.
Leave the cell phone alone.

narration.text: Avoid distraction by fixing your eyes on the road with your hands on the wheel, presetting every control before you start rolling, and leaving the cell phone alone. Eyes-up, preset and phone-down habits buy back the recognition seconds that distraction eats. If something does need your attention while you drive, the manual's rule is to pull fully over before any distracting act, and the device law adds that you hold nothing and enter nothing. Remember why those seconds matter: distraction causes roughly seventeen percent of Virginia crashes, because the straying car enters danger, recognition lags precious seconds, and an emergency move follows.

lines.text: Phone mounted for navigation.
Want to type a new address.
Legal while driving?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lia's phone is showing her navigation, and she wants to type a new address into the map app while driving. Is that legal? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Navigation use stands only while entering nothing and holding nothing, and Virginia bars holding a phone or wireless device at the wheel, except in a driver emergency or while lawfully parked or stopped. Lia should pull fully over, enter the address, and then drive on with the phone hands-free. The manual's broader rule is the same: pull fully over before any distracting act. Hold nothing, enter nothing.

lines.text: Shelve devices except for emergencies.
No holding a phone; navigation hands-free only.
Eyes up, controls preset, phone down.

narration.text: To close the lesson: driving wants your whole attention, so shelve phones, computers and similar devices except to report a crash or emergency, and pull fully over before any distracting act. Virginia bars holding a phone or wireless device at the wheel, except in a driver emergency or while lawfully parked or stopped, and navigation is allowed only while entering nothing and holding nothing. Distraction causes roughly seventeen percent of Virginia crashes, because recognition lags precious seconds. Prevent it by keeping your eyes on the road and hands on the wheel, presetting every control before rolling, and leaving the cell phone alone. Hold nothing, enter nothing.

correction.text: Near deer call for slowing, horns and group wariness, while certain contact calls for straight-line braking with no swerve.

lines.text: At the scene.
Information and reports.
Unattended cars and deer.

narration.text: Welcome to the last lesson of this section, on crashes and animal strikes. The manual gives step-by-step instructions for the crash scene: where to stop, when to move the cars, how to help the injured, and when to call police. It lists the information to exchange, when to call your insurer, and when officers file reports with DMV. It sets out what to do if you hit an empty car or other property. And it explains how to avoid deer and other large animals, and what to do when hitting one cannot be avoided. Every one of these situations requires a report of some kind, so we will pay close attention to who gets told and when.

lines.text: Stop at or near the scene without blocking traffic.
Clear drivable cars when no one is hurt and it is safe.
Help the hurt without moving them; summon police.

narration.text: In a crash, stop at the scene or near it, without blocking traffic. If the cars are drivable, nobody is hurt and it is safe, move them out of the road. Step out on the side shielded by your car. Help anyone who is hurt, but do not move them unless you are trained or there is a fire danger. And summon police quickly, since property, injury and fatal crashes all require reports. Put as a contrast: drivable and unhurt means clear the road at once, while hurt occupants mean shield, aid and summon without moving them. The deciding questions are whether anyone is hurt and whether the cars can be moved safely.

lines.text: Trade names, addresses, license and plate numbers.
Injured and witness contacts; insurance policy numbers.
Officers report injury, death, damage over three thousand dollars.

narration.text: At the scene, exchange names, addresses, license and plate numbers, contact details for injured people and witnesses, and the owners' insurance policy numbers. Call your insurer at once. Officers file DMV reports on any crash with injury or death, or with damage over three thousand dollars, and those reports are entered on every involved driver's record. So injury, death or damage over three thousand dollars routes to DMV records. Notice that the report goes on every involved driver's record. The insurance call is your own duty, and the manual says to make it at once.

lines.text: Look reasonably for the owner.
Leave a note: name, phone, date, time, damage sketch.
Still tell police within twenty-four hours.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver hits an empty parked car, leaves a note, and thinks the job is done. The manual adds one more step. After striking an empty car or other property, hunt reasonably for its owner. If you cannot find them, leave an easy-to-find note with your name, phone number, the date and time, and a sketch of the damage. And still tell police within twenty-four hours. Put as a contrast: manned crashes trade papers and call insurers on the spot, while empty-car strikes leave name-phone-time notes plus a twenty-four-hour police report. The note and the police report are both required, not one or the other.

lines.text: Tens of thousands of strikes a year in Virginia.
Watch at dusk and dawn through fall.
Brake for groups; use the horn to move them off.

narration.text: Tens of thousands of deer, elk and bear strikes happen in Virginia each year. Stay sharp at dusk and dawn, especially through the fall. Brake for groups of animals near the road, and use your horn to move them off. When contact is certain, hold your lane under firm braking to a controlled stop instead of swerving. Then report a large-animal strike to police. So any large-animal strike routes to law enforcement, much as injury, death or damage over three thousand dollars routes to DMV records. The two reporting rules sit side by side: crashes with injury or big damage reach DMV records, and large-animal strikes are reported to police.

lines.text: Hit a parked car.
Owner cannot be found.
Is a note enough?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Raj backs into a parked car and cannot find its owner after looking. He leaves a note. Is that enough? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. After striking an empty car, you look reasonably for the owner, and if you cannot find them, you leave an easy-to-find note with your name, phone, the date, the time and a damage sketch, and you still tell police within twenty-four hours. Raj needs to make that police report too. Compare a crash where the other driver is present, where you trade papers on the spot and call your insurer. A note plus a police report within twenty-four hours is the empty-car rule.

lines.text: Stop, clear if safe, help, call police.
Exchange information; call your insurer.
Deer certain: brake straight, no swerve.

narration.text: To close the section: in a crash, stop at or near the scene without blocking traffic, move drivable cars when nobody is hurt and it is safe, help the injured without moving them unless trained or there is a fire danger, and summon police. Exchange names, addresses, license and plate numbers, witness contacts and insurance policy numbers, and call your insurer at once. Officers file DMV reports for injury, death or damage over three thousand dollars. After hitting an empty car, leave a note and tell police within twenty-four hours. With deer, slow and use the horn, and when a hit is certain, brake firmly in your lane instead of swerving, then report it.
